FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Compare and determine the basics of various study types (cohort, case-control, cross-
sectional, randomized, meta-analysis).
Assess the level of evidence for various study types.
Identify measurable outcomes in clinical research.
Define biases in clinical research.
Clinical Study Design
Observation Study
Researchers collect data from patients for whom the decision about exposures is self-chosen
or is a combined decision made between the patient and his or her physician, which frequently
is the case. Observation studies can be prospective or retrospective (Resource 1).

In prospective studies, new data are collected from the outset of the study forward.
Retrospective studies collect data that already exist.
If some data of interest already exist, a combination of prospective and retrospective data
collection can be used (eg, through health records); however, additional data and/or outcomes
also are collected in a prospective manner.
Experimental Study
Researchers expose participants to some type of therapeutic, preventive, or diagnostic
intervention.
Any experimental study is prospective by nature.
Cohort Studies
Observational-Type Study
In a cohort study, a group of patients is selected and observed over a period of time (Resource
2).
Observation can be done prospectively (patients are identified by the investigator and
followed into the future), or retrospectively (patients are identified, and their past records are
examined).
The objective of a prospective cohort study is to measure or record potential predictors (risk
factors, especially modifiable ones) of outcomes and follow up with the patients periodically to
determine patient outcomes.
Strengths
The greatest advantage of a prospective cohort study is that the results identify the prognosis
and risk factors (predictors) of outcomes. Cohort studies also have the important advantage of
providing the appropriate information to determine incidence.
An additional advantage of the prospective cohort study is that the lack of knowledge of the
outcome (its presence or absence, characteristics about it) reduces the potential for bias in the
measurement of the predictors. Therefore, variable measurement in prospective studies
typically is more accurate and complete than that used in retrospective studies.
The risk of recall bias, in which patients with the outcome remember a predictor
disproportionately better than patients without the outcome, is substantially reduced in

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001009
2/23

prospective studies compared with retrospective studies.
Weaknesses
Confounding is an important issue in cohort studies. Confounders are variables that are
related to the outcome and the predictor, and they can cause associations or predictions to be
erroneous. These variables or potential risk factors are controlled for in multivariable analyses
but may be difficult to control for in smaller observation studies, including cohort studies.
However, with careful hypotheses and an understanding of the disease processes, an
investigator can account for confounders by including them in the model if the sample size is
large enough to allow many variables to be tested and/or included. Unknown confounders
cannot be controlled for in modeling. This factor demonstrates a major statistical advantage of
a randomized controlled trial (RCT).
In retrospective cohort studies, the ability to control follow-up time and the sampling of the
population are limited.
Concerns also exist about the quality and accuracy of measurements obtained at baseline.
Statistics
Most prospective and retrospective cohort studies require multivariate modeling.
The effects of a cohort study also can be reported as relative risk.
Example
Multicenter Orthopaedics Outcome Network study1,2
More than 3,500 patients who underwent anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR)
were enrolled in this study. Preoperative patient variables, patient-reported outcome
measures (PROMs), and intraoperative variables were collected. Outcomes were collected at
2, 6, and 10 years postoperatively.
From this cohort, numerous important insights have been gained, including the ACLR
prognosis for PROMs at 10 years postoperatively and the modifiable risk factors of PROMs at
that time. PROMs initially were measured at 2 years postoperatively and stayed constant at
6-year and 10-year follow-up. Risk factors predicting poorer outcomes included lower
baseline scores on PROMs, a higher body mass index, smoking, having undergone surgery
for the management of meniscal pathology before index ACLR, having undergone lateral

meniscectomy during index ACLR, having undergone revision ACLR, grade 3 or grade 4
articular cartilage defects of any knee compartment, and having undergone a subsequent
surgical procedure on the ipsilateral knee after index ACLR.
Case-Control Study
Observational-Type Study
Case-control studies are conducted so that two groups of patients—one group with the
outcome (also known as cases) and one group without the outcome (also known as the control
group)—are included in the study (Resources 1 and 2).
Predictors are compared between the two groups to determine which predictors influence the
outcome.
Ideally, the controls are matched with the cases on important predictors, such as age and sex.
This type of design is optimal for studying rare outcomes or diseases.
Cohort studies can be prospective or retrospective, whereas case-control studies are mainly
retrospective. They always identify a group with the disease or outcome and a group without
the disease or outcome. Then the investigators look back in time to judge the differences
between the groups with respect to potential predictors (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Chart shows the design of a case-control study. (Reproduced from Gagnier JJ:
Principles of clinical studies, in Aaron RK, ed: Orthopaedic Basic Science: Foundations of Clinical
Practice, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 505-517.)
Strengths
The advantage of case-control studies is that groups are self-chosen. Therefore, the
investigators can assess any outcome and related exposure and can easily study rare
outcomes or outcomes that take a long time to develop.
The primary outcome in this study type is an odds ratio, which represents an approximate
strength of the association between the outcome and the predictor variable.
Weaknesses
Only a single disease or outcome can be examined at a time, whereas multiple outcome
variables can be examined in cohort studies.
Another weakness of the case-control design is that it cannot provide insight into prevalence
or incidence because the proportion of cases to controls is determined by the investigator
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Research Methodology and Study Design
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001009
5/23

during the study design.
Finally, and most importantly, bias is a more serious concern in case-control studies than in
cohort studies. Not only is selection bias a concern, but recall bias—in which patients who
have a condition may recall their exposure to a predictor better than the controls—also is a
problem.
Example
In a case-control study, Sturnick et al3 recruited 88 patients with a first-time anterior cruciate
ligament (ACL) tear and 88 matched-control subjects who were uninjured. Each subject
enrolled underwent MRI of the injured knee (patients) or the corresponding knee (matched
controls). In addition, measurements were determined for the size of the ACL and the femoral
intercondylar notch.
Multivariate logistic modeling was performed to determine the risk of noncontact ACL injury in
males and females. The modeling showed that, for males, the highest risk of noncontact ACL
injury was incurred with a decreased ACL volume and a decreased wedge angle in the lateral
compartment between the posterior meniscus and the subchondral bone. The anatomic
factors that led to the greatest increased risk of noncontact ACL injury in females were a
decreased width of the femoral notch and an increased slope of the tibial articular cartilage,
when measured in a posteroinferior direction.
Cross-Sectional Study
Observational-Type Study
The cross-sectional study design provides insight into the population being studied at a single
point or moment in time. Therefore, this study type is best suited for descriptive studies rather
than predictive studies (Resources 1 and 2).
When using a cross-sectional design to gain descriptive information, the investigator must
recognize that only prevalence, and not incidence, can be determined. Prevalence describes
the number of patients in a population who have a condition at a single point in time, whereas
incidence is defined as the proportion of the population who have newly developed the
condition over a set period of time. Prevalence holds substantial weight in the clinical
environment, because it informs clinicians about a patient’s likelihood of having a certain
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Research Methodology and Study Design
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001009
6/23

condition before obtaining a thorough work-up, which, in statistical language, is called the
patient’s prior probability of having the disease.
Strengths
Convenience is one of the major strengths of a cross-sectional design because these studies
are quick to complete and relatively inexpensive. Therefore, this type of study often is included
as an initial component of RCTs or cohort studies.
One common reason for taking this approach is to obtain information, including demographic
data, about the patients at baseline.
Weaknesses
Determining causal relationships is quite difficult with this approach, especially because of the
lack of time-related data. Whether a factor has a causative influence on a disease or merely is
associated with the disease being present may be difficult to determine.
Studying rare diseases or rare events is difficult with this study type; the cross-sectional design
is impractical because of the exceptionally large sample size that would be required.
Example
The importance of understanding prevalence is shown in the cross-sectional study by Sher et
al,4 in which MRI findings from 96 asymptomatic shoulders were described. The study
reported that 54% of patients (25 of 46) older than 60 years with an asymptomatic shoulder
had a rotator cuff tear visible on MRI, 52% of which (13 of 25) were full-thickness tears
(Resource 3).
The high prevalence of rotator cuff tears in patients with an asymptomatic shoulder is a
reminder to clinicians to be exercise caution in attributing the rotator cuff as the only cause of
shoulder pain and symptoms.
Case Series
Observational-Type Study
A series of patients is presented with outcomes but without a control population or
comparison group (Resources 1 and 4).

7/23

This type of study design, although frequently used in orthopaedic literature, provides a low
level of evidence because it includes no control group and the population usually is poorly
defined.
This type of study may be helpful as a starting point for additional analysis and may generate a
hypothesis.
Strengths
This type of study often drives hypotheses and provides estimates for a treatment’s effect size
and its standard deviation, which may inform power analyses for comparative, prospective
trials.
Importantly, this type of study may alert the clinical community about treatments that have a
high incidence of failure and a likelihood of patient harm.
Weaknesses
No control group
Can easily be affected by selection bias
Cannot determine the incidence and prevalence of cases
Example
Churchill et al5 described a series in which surgeons successfully repaired articular cartilage
defects in the knee.
Included in the study were 10 patients who underwent primary repair via internal fixation and
showed excellent radiographic, PROMs, and return to sports.
Randomized Controlled Trials
Experimental-Type Study
The best experimental design for establishing cause-and-effect relationships is the RCT. RCTs
have distinct features (Resources 1, 4, and 5)
The outcomes of interest are not present at the time of enrollment into the study; they are
prospective.
SEND FEEDBACK

8/23

A concurrent control or comparison group is used, assignment to the groups is random
(obtained via random number generator), and the exposure to groups is under the control of
the investigator (experimental).
RCTs can compare an active intervention with a placebo, no intervention, or some other
active intervention. The latter type would be a comparative effectiveness study.
Clinical equipoise—the assumption that no reasonable basis exists for choosing one
intervention over another in a specific patient—is necessary if comparing two interventions.
Types
Parallel design
The study population is randomly divided into groups, with each subject in each group
exposed to only one intervention.
Typically, one of the interventions is a new drug or treatment that is being tested.
One group is treated with the new intervention, and the other group, which is considered
the control group, is treated with either no treatment or another treatment that is
considered the benchmark.
The groups are then compared to determine if one intervention is superior at achieving a
particular outcome of interest (Figure 2; Resource 5).
Figure 2 Diagram shows the concept of parallel design. (Reproduced from Lin HA, Henry
PDG, Wasserstein D: Randomized controlled trials, in Aaron RK, ed: Orthopaedic Basic
Science: Foundations of Clinical Practice, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 525-537.)
Crossover design
Two or more groups receive the same intervention(s), but at different times, with a washout
period in between. In this case, the subjects serve as their own controls.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Research Methodology and Study Design
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001009
9/23

A major advantage of the crossover design is the avoidance of confounders (eg, age or sex)
within the study and control groups because the same people make up each group. This
arrangement leads to statistical efficiency because fewer patients (smaller sample size) are
required.
The disadvantages of crossover RCTs include a longer study duration, difficulty in managing
patients who drop out and complete only a single evaluation phase, the possibility of
unblinding if the participants noticed sizeable differences between the treatment phases,
and the possibility of carryover effects between evaluation phases, especially if the washout
phase is insufficient (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Diagram shows the design and progress of a crossover study involving two or
more groups. (Reproduced from Lin HA, Henry PDG, Wasserstein D: Randomized controlled
trials, in Aaron RK, ed: Orthopaedic Basic Science: Foundations of Clinical Practice, ed 5.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 525-537.)
Randomization
Randomization is the process of randomly allocating patients into groups within a study.
This process aims to reduce selection bias.
Randomization increases the likelihood of a balanced profile of subjects within each group,
including known and unknown demographic, confounding, or prognostic factors, so the
groups differ only in the interventions to be compared.
The theoretic balancing of unknown confounding factors is a substantial advantage of the
RCT over matched, nonrandomized prospective studies, in which the likelihood of unknown
confounders is higher and may influence the results.
Analysis
Intention-to-treat analysis
Patients are analyzed according to the groups into which they are randomized.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Research Methodology and Study Design
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001009
10/23

Intention-to-treat analysis best maintains the balances of known and unknown prognostic
factors, but it may underestimate the size of the treatment effect if substantial crossover
exists between groups.
Per protocol analysis
Patients are analyzed according to the treatment that they actually received.
Per protocol analysis may overestimate or underestimate the effect size, because the
randomization is compromised.
Strengths
The major advantage of the RCT is the randomization process, which theoretically equally
distributes all uncontrolled variables between the groups if the sample size is large enough.
RCTs are able to establish a cause and effect relationship and can clearly and definitely answer
a primary study question.
Weaknesses
Random allocation is not always possible if random assignment to a certain exposure may be
unethical (eg, harmful exposure).
RCTs also take a long time to complete, are expensive, and frequently require large sample
sizes, and they typically are not suitable for the study of distant or rare events.
Frequently, these studies have narrow selection criteria; therefore, the results may not be able
to be generalized broadly.
Example
The Meniscal Tear in Osteoarthritis Research trial6
A multicenter RCT comparing arthroscopic partial meniscectomy with physical therapy in
patients with a meniscal tear and mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis. A total of 351
patients were assigned randomly to surgical treatment and postoperative physical therapy or
to standardized physical therapy (with the option to cross over).
In the intention-to-treat analysis, no substantial differences were observed between the
study groups with regard to functional improvement 6 months after randomization;
however, 30% of the patients who were assigned to physical therapy alone underwent
surgical treatment within 6 months.

Reviews and Meta-analyses
Narrative Review
Summarizes the literature selected by an author or group of experts (based on author opinion)
of relevance to a topic of interest (Resource 6).
Narrative reviews are useful for providing a broad overview of the evaluation and
management of a particular condition, for offering historical context, and for describing new
developments or the state of the art in a particular area.
A narrative review is inherently biased.
The method of selecting studies is unlikely to be objective or systematic.
Relevant data, findings, or publications may be presented selectively or omitted, and
interpretation usually is qualitative and based on opinion or experience.
Systematic Review
A scientific investigation of the published literature.
Published studies are the subjects in this type of research.
Systematic reviews use defined strategies for the identification, inclusion, appraisal, and
reporting of results to summarize the literature addressing one or more specific clinical
questions.
The purpose of a systematic review is to answer a specific question using published
information, favoring the highest level of available evidence.
Strengths
Provides a methodic, up-to-date answer to a clinical question by pooling results from multiple
studies to compare treatment options, diagnostic tests, or measures of outcome.
Weaknesses
Sensitive to publication bias.
Published trials in orthopaedic surgery are more likely to describe positive treatment effects
rather than negative or null treatment effects.
Negative results are less likely to be published, and unpublished results are impossible to
include in a systematic review.

12/23

Therefore, the efficacy of a treatment or treatment effect may be overestimated by a
methodologically sound systematic review that has captured selectively published positive
results.
Meta-analysis
A meta-analysis is the quantitative analysis of data from a systematic review of the literature. It
uses statistical methods to pool results from different trials that may have been performed
across different practice settings and, therefore, in different patient populations. Therefore,
these pooled data may exhibit better external validity than that of an individual trial. The
results provide the highest level of evidence.
Traditional meta-analyses are referred to as pairwise meta-analyses. They pool results from
RCTs that directly compare two interventions. These analyses provide greater precision in
estimating treatment effects and often have the power to perform subgroup analyses,
evaluate the heterogeneity across studies, and assist in future hypothesis generation.
The quality of evidence produced from a properly conducted systematic review or meta-
analysis is only as good as the quality of the studies included. Therefore, the level of evidence
is based on the lowest level of evidence of the studies analyzed.
Strengths
Meta-analysis improves the power of the statistical analysis, increasing the precision of the
result.
Greater precision increases the likelihood that any association or difference may be
interpreted as statistically significant.
Weaknesses
Pooling similar studies to improve power may sacrifice validity if heterogeneity among the
studies is present. Heterogeneity refers to differences between studies in selection criteria,
characteristics of the sample populations, exposures or interventions, methods of allocating
patients to exposures or interventions, distributions of potentially confounding variables
across the exposure/intervention and control groups, blinding of the study patients or
outcome assessments, outcome assessment techniques, timing of outcome assessment, data
collection methods, follow-up, or any other study characteristic or method that differs

13/23

between studies in a manner that may affect—and therefore influence—the measured
outcome.
Similar to systematic reviews, these designs are sensitive to publication bias.
Example
Minkara et al7 performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of outcomes after hip
arthroscopy for the management of femoroacetabular impingement. Using Preferred
Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses guidelines, the investigators
included 31 articles after applying inclusion and exclusion criteria. After combining the 1,911
patients included in these studies, the pooled outcomes were obtained for revision surgery,
complications, PROMs, and risk factors.
The authors concluded that a high percentage of patients returned to sports activity after hip
arthroscopy for the management of femoroacetabular impingement, with a low rate of
complications and revision surgery. All PROMs, except for mental health, substantially
improved postoperatively.
Levels of Evidence of Clinical Studies
In considering the effect of research studies, it is important to consider the amount of weight
each type of study carries in changing clinical practice.
A well-established hierarchy of study types, which has been summarized by the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Evidence-Based Practice Committee, has been
established.8
Levels of evidence provide a quick appraisal of study quality and can be used to develop
practice guidelines9 (Resource 7).
The most influential therapeutic study, which is considered level I evidence, is a high-quality
RCT with narrow confidence intervals.
The most influential prognostic study is a high-quality prospective cohort study, in which all
patients are enrolled at the same time, with more than 80% follow-up.
Meta-analyses and systematic reviews of all level I studies also are considered level I evidence.
Clinically important results from higher level of evidence studies allow surgeons to change
their practices accordingly (Table 1; Resource 8).

Measuring Outcomes
Relevant and precise outcome measurement tools should be used to assess treatment effects.
The simplest outcome measurements are dichotomous, meaning that the outcome of
interest is either present or absent. Examples include survival, revision surgery, and
infection.
Judging whether these outcomes are present may be subject to interpretation in some cases.
If the outcome assessor is not blinded to treatment, information bias may be introduced.
PROMs are questionnaires completed by patients to assess their perception of health,
function, and quality of life.
Three types of PROMs are available: generic, joint-specific, and disease-specific.
Generic PROMs aim to assess a patient’s general health status by measuring multiple
domains and are valuable in comparing health across a range of disease processes.
Generic PROM examples

Bias in Clinical Research
Bias is defined as the systematic deviation from the truth and may arise at any stage of clinical
research.
Bias takes many forms, including selection bias, performance bias, detection bias, attrition
bias, reporting bias, and bias resulting from conflicts of interest (eg, from the funding source
or intellectual property; Table 3).

Selection bias
Occurs if participant sampling results in unequal baseline and demographic characteristics
in groups being compared.
Such bias can occur in observational studies because patients are not allocated to
interventions.
Selection bias is mitigated in randomized studies via the allocation methods and random
assignment so baseline characteristics of both comparison groups are similar.
Detection bias
Systematic differences in how outcomes are measured between groups.
In all prospective clinical research, blinding of the outcome assessors and carefully
performing outcomes assessments the same way for each group may mitigate this type of
bias.
Attrition bias
Systematic differences in the withdrawals from a study or from incomplete data (eg,
missing data points for multiple follow-ups).
Withdrawals or incomplete data arise because of attrition (patients are lost to follow-up for
various reasons) and exclusion (patients are withdrawn from the study after initial inclusion
and participation in the study). In both scenarios, the loss of outcome data may
systematically alter the data and introduce bias into the comparisons.
Several methods exist to mitigate bias because of attrition, such as imputation methods for
missing data (a computer program that fills in the missing data) and sensitivity analysis (eg,
conducting separate analyses for those with missing data versus those with no missing
data to examine the influence of the missing data).
In RCTs, intention-to-treat analyses preserve the randomization process so that patients
are analyzed in the groups to which they were originally allocated—even if they did not
actually receive the intervention at all or in part—to control for attrition bias.
